nodes.name: WO3 nanosheet synthesis
nodes.procedure: Firstly, 20 mL 1 M NaWO4 aqueous solution was added into a 180 mL 3 M HCl solution by drop with stirring. After the mix solution aged for 1h, the precipitate was washed by deionized water and alcohol until the pH was about 7. The obtained precipitate WO3·2H2O was then dried in a vacuum drying oven at 60°C for 12h. Then the WO3 nanosheets were acquired by putting WO3·2H2O into a tube furnace and annealing at 350°C for 1h.

nodes.name: Pt-WO3 photochemical synthesis
nodes.procedure: Firstly, 50 mg WO3 nanosheets were dispersed into 50 mL deionized water and put into an ultrasonic machine for ultrasonic dispersion about 10 min. Then, 100 μL 20 mg mL⁻¹ H₂PtCl₆·6H₂O solution was added into above WO3 dispersed solution with stirring. 20 min later, the mix solution was exposed under the simulated solar irradiation from a Xenon lamp with stirring. After photochemical reaction for 2 h, the synthesized Pt-WO3 sample was then washed by deionized water and dried in vacuum oven. Pt-WO3 with other Pt wt.% were prepared by adding different amount of H₂PtCl₆·6H₂O solution.

nodes.characterization_summary: SEM images show that the morphology of WO3 nanosheets does not change before and after Pt loading.
nodes.evidence_snippet: Scanning electron microscopy (SEM) images as displayed in Fig. S2 show that the morphology of WO3 nanosheets does not change before and after Pt loading.

nodes.characterization_summary: ICP-OES measured platinum contents in Pt-WO3 catalysts vary from 0.365 wt% to 4.426 wt%, with the detailed sample at 1.401 wt%.
nodes.evidence_snippet: Inductively coupled plasma optical emission spectrometry (ICP-OES) was applied to measure the platinum contents in the Pt-WO3 catalysts... platinum contents vary from 0.365 wt% to 4.426 wt% for these samples, in which the sample with 1.401 wt% Pt was investigated in detail.

nodes.characterization_summary: XRD pattern of Pt-WO3 matches WO3 (PDF#83-0951) with no platinum diffraction peaks discernible, indicating no crystalline Pt nanostructure.
nodes.evidence_snippet: As shown in Fig. 1a and Fig. S3a, the X-ray diffraction (XRD) pattern of Pt-WO3 matches with that of WO3 (PDF#83-0951) with no platinum diffraction peaks discernible.

nodes.characterization_summary: Pt 4f XPS shows Pt mainly present as +2 (72.6 eV 4f5/2, 76.0 eV 4f7/2) and +4 (78.1 eV 4f7/2) with absence of metallic Pt0; O 1s shows W-O bonds at 530.3 eV and Pt-O bonds at 530.9 eV.
nodes.evidence_snippet: As shown in Fig. 1b, the Pt atoms in Pt-WO3 are mainly present as +2 and +4. The peak with binding energy of 78.1 eV can be assigned to 4f7/2 of Pt4+ and the two peaks at 72.6 eV and 76.0 eV belong to 4f5/2 and 4f7/2 of Pt2+. ... two peaks in the O 1s XPS spectrum in Fig. 1c can be ascribed to W-O bonds (530.3 eV) and Pt-O bonds (530.9 eV).

nodes.characterization_summary: HAADF-STEM shows lighter spots of Pt clusters; lattice spacings of 0.377 nm (020) and 0.365 nm (200) confirm WO3 (002) exposed plane with atomically doped Pt clusters.
nodes.evidence_snippet: In Fig. 1d, some lighter spots are observed, which can be assigned to the platinum clusters... the spacing of the two orthogonal lattice planes are measured about 0.377 nm and 0.365 nm, corresponding the (020) and (200) facets of WO3, respectively.

nodes.characterization_summary: CV shows redox peaks for H+ insertion/disinsertion in WO3 (0.3-0 V) and Pt hydrogen adsorption (0.3-0.1 V); positive shift of reduction peak at ~0.2 V for Pt-WO3.
nodes.evidence_snippet: As shown in Fig. 2c, the CV curves of Pt-WO3 and WO3 exhibit different redox peaks... the redox peaks between 0.3 and 0 V for WO3 can be assigned to H+ insertion and disinsertion in WO3.

nodes.characterization_summary: In-situ Raman shows WO3 peaks at 268 cm⁻¹, 710 cm⁻¹, 806 cm⁻¹ disappear from 0.1 V to 0.05 V (vs. RHE) then reappear, verifying reversible phase transition to HxWO3.
nodes.evidence_snippet: As shown in Fig. 2e and f, the peaks at 268 cm⁻¹, 710 cm⁻¹ and 806 cm⁻¹ can be assigned to the characteristic peaks of surface W-O bonds of WO3. The Raman characteristic peaks of WO3 disappear with applied potential from 0.1 V to 0.05 V (vs. RHE) and then re-appear.

nodes.characterization_summary: In-situ EIS shows Pt-WO3 has smaller charge transfer resistance than Pt-TiO2; two arcs indicate inner-layer (Rc) and interface (Rct) processes; HxWO3 enables fast electron transfer.
nodes.evidence_snippet: As shown in Fig. 3a, the Nyquist plots were collected at HER overpotential of 40 mV. Obviously, the much smaller circle arcs for Pt-WO3 and Pt/C indicate much smaller resistances in their electrode systems.

nodes.characterization_summary: Post-HER XPS shows Pt 4f spectrum with Pt0 species as real active sites after in-situ reduction from +2/+4 to 0.
nodes.evidence_snippet: In Fig. 2d, the Pt 4f XPS spectrum indicates that the Pt0 species are the real active sites when catalyzing HER.
